body:
WHAT
A shell command that stops processes BY NAME, or every process, never runs unasked.
- The classifier (bashProcessKillSubject, used by Bash and by Monitor, which runs a shell too) looks at each simple command — after ;, &&, ||, |, &, a newline, (, {, $( or a backtick, and through sudo / env / nohup / time / xargs / bash -c / cmd /c / powershell -Command. It flags: taskkill with /IM (also //IM and -IM) or with no /PID at all; pkill; killall; tskill <name>; Stop-Process / spps (and PowerShell's `kill -Name`) unless it names only ids and is not fed by a pipe; a POSIX kill whose target is -1 (every process); wmic process … delete or call terminate; a Win32_Process terminate; and any kill that gets its pids from a name lookup in the same command (pgrep, pidof, ps, Get-Process, tasklist). It does NOT flag: kills by pid (taskkill /PID 1234, kill 1234, kill -TERM $!, Stop-Process -Id 1234); kills by port (fuser -k, lsof -ti:3000 | xargs kill, npx kill-port); listing (pgrep, tasklist, ps aux | grep …); or the word inside an argument (grep kill, git commit -m "… pkill …", killed.txt, .claude/skills).
- Outside OVERDRIVE a flagged call asks, as the process-kill guard, right after deny rules. The prompt's description is "Stops processes by name — every matching process on this computer, not only the ones this session started." and its subject is the command. "Always allow" remembers that exact command only, never its shape; "allow session" allows this call only. A decline reaches the model as an error that names TaskStop and pids.
- In OVERDRIVE, where nothing may ask, a flagged call is refused without a prompt, and the refusal names TaskStop and pids.
- In both stances the one standing override is a literal grant or an explicit subject rule for that exact command (e.g. Bash(taskkill /F /IM myapp.exe)). A bare Bash rule, Bash(*), a session allow, or a command-shape grant never covers it. The "Allow deletions" switch does not turn it off: a kill is not a deletion.
- A command that is both a kill by name and a deletion asks for the kill first and then for the deletion; a note attached to either approval reaches the model.
- The desktop approval card (single console and tiled pane) shows the guard's line under the command; the TUI prompt already shows a request's description.
- Resolution order becomes: deny rules > process-kill guard > protected-path guard > deletion guard > allow rules > stance default.

WHY
Field test 2026-09-23, finding S-01 (docs/reports/2026-09-23-magentra-field-test). In OVERDRIVE the agent ran `cd /c/Users/alini/phdworks/test && (taskkill //F //IM python.exe //FI "WINDOWTITLE eq *" 2>/dev/null; true) | head -n 2; sleep 1; echo done` with no prompt; the transcript records decision allow, source mode. That stops every python.exe on the computer, not only the game server. Four seconds later the agent used TaskStop on its own job. No kill form was classified anywhere, so the stance default (allow) ran it, and OVERDRIVE computes no deletion subject at all.

WHERE
engine/tools/src/bash.ts — bashProcessKillSubject(), bashTool.processKillSubject, and the new Bash description bullet ("- To stop a background command, use TaskStop with its task id. Never stop processes by name (taskkill /IM, pkill, killall, Stop-Process -Name): that stops every matching process on the machine, not only yours.", owner-approved 2026-09-23). engine/tools/src/monitor.ts — monitorTool.processKillSubject. engine/core/src/agent/tool.ts — ToolDefinition.processKillSubject. engine/core/src/runtime/permissions.ts — the new block in PermissionEngine.check, ApprovalSource "process-kill-guard". engine/core/src/runtime/session.ts — the transcript source for that approval. app/renderer/modules/landing.js fillPermissionModal(), app/renderer/modules/tabs.js showPaneApproval() — the guard's line on the card.

TEST CHECKLIST
1. (pure) The classifier flags the field command verbatim and every form listed as flagged under WHAT, and passes over every form listed as not flagged.
2. (pure) Outside OVERDRIVE, with Bash allowed outright, a flagged call asks exactly once, as the process-kill guard; the request's description is the guard's line and its subject is the command. A decline refuses with a message that names TaskStop.
3. (pure) In OVERDRIVE a flagged call is refused and nothing asks; the refusal names TaskStop and OVERDRIVE.
4. (pure) A bare Bash rule, Bash(*), a session allow and a command-shape grant never cover a kill by name, in either stance; switching the deletion guard off does not switch this guard off.
5. (pure) "Always allow" on a kill prompt grants that literal command only: the same command then runs with no prompt, a variant still asks. An explicit rule for the exact command runs it with no prompt in both stances.
6. (pure) A command that is a kill by name and a deletion asks twice, kill first; the note attached to the kill approval reaches the model.
7. (proc) A real session with a real shell, whose model issues the field-shaped command against a process name that cannot exist followed by a marker-file write: in OVERDRIVE the tool result is the refusal, no permission_request is sent, and the marker is never written. Outside OVERDRIVE the same call asks; declined, the marker is absent; approved, it is written.
8. (ui) In the real app, a permission_request from the guard shows the guard's line under the command, in the single-console card and in a tiled pane; an ordinary deletion prompt shows no extra line.
